section_summary: This section combines press summaries and diplomatic correspondence on Japan with records of U.S. efforts to control strategic exports, including cobalt, scrap rails, aviation materials, and other war supplies. Its largest subfile is a Colombian government geological report evaluating the Playas zinc deposit near Junín, its mineralogy, estimated reserves, transport conditions, and proposed exploration works. The remaining documents investigate cobalt imported from Canada and then shipped to Japan, answer a congressional inquiry about export restrictions, consider a Costa Rican rail-for-locomotives transaction, and record evidence of unusually large Japanese purchases in the United States.

subfiles.title: Telegram summarizing American press comment on Japan and Ambassador Grew
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo, via Shanghai; repeated to Peiping and Chungking
subfiles.about: The telegram transmits American newspaper reactions to Japanese alignment with the Axis, Japanese expansion, Ambassador Grew's remarks, and Foreign Minister Matsuoka's assurances.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers call for tighter restrictions or an embargo on strategic exports to Japan and dismiss Japanese claims that its Asian program is peaceful or mutually beneficial. Editorials praise Ambassador Grew for clearly communicating American concern about Japanese conduct in China. Further commentary argues that Matsuoka's conciliatory language is contradicted by Japan's occupation policies, attacks on American interests, and alliance with Germany and Italy.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on aluminum products manufactured in China
subfiles.about: The note points to a memorandum reporting measures by Chinese Aluminum Rolling Mills, Limited, to prevent Japanese acquisition of its products.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Chinese Aluminum Rolling Mills acted to block purchases by Japanese parties.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1243 on the availability of zinc ore in Colombia
subfiles.about: The embassy forwards a Colombian geological study and reports efforts to market Colombian zinc outside Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1243 encloses a study of a Cundinamarca zinc deposit; Ernesto Medina reported Japanese interest, but U.S. shipping, smelting and duty costs seem prohibitive.

subfiles.title: Report on the Playas zinc deposit, Municipality of Junín, Cundinamarca
subfiles.from: Benjamin Alvarado and Clímaco Palau, Commission on Mineral Studies
subfiles.to: Colombian Ministry of Mines and Petroleum
subfiles.about: The report evaluates the geology, mineralization, possible reserves, exploration requirements, and commercial prospects of the Playas zinc deposit.
subfiles.summary: The investigators describe a fault-controlled sphalerite deposit at El Rincón, associated with siderite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, arsenopyrite, and minor galena, and relate transported ore blocks near Quebrada Negra to the same possible vein system. They conclude that the mineralization was produced by hot magmatic or hydrothermal solutions and may extend roughly three kilometers toward Llano Grande, while emphasizing that the available outcrops do not prove its continuity or grade. Speculative calculations suggest substantial tonnage, but the authors recommend underground drifts, crosscuts, and magnetometer surveys before reliable reserve estimates can be made. They also discuss access to Bogotá and export ports, hydroelectric power, coal, labor, costs, and the justification for further technical exploration.

subfiles.title: Treasury letter transmitting cobalt-shipment investigation reports
subfiles.from: Herbert E. Gaston, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: The Treasury forwards Customs reports on Canadian cobalt products imported into the United States and subsequently sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Treasury sends two New York customs reports on whether cobalt transactions violated Canada's understanding that it was for U.S. defense use.

subfiles.title: Customs report on the first Canadian cobalt shipment to Japan
subfiles.from: Gordon H. Pike, U.S. Customs Service
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Investigations and Patrol
subfiles.about: The report traces 378 bags of Canadian arsenical cobalt concentrates through New Jersey warehouses to shipment aboard the Asosan Maru for Osaka.
subfiles.summary: Customs: five Canadian cobalt lots entered at Niagara Falls reached Metal & Ore Corporation; the first 378 bags went to Mitsui and on the Asosan Maru, which cleared October 28 for Osaka.

subfiles.title: Follow-up Customs report on Canadian cobalt exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Gordon H. Pike and E. J. Dougherty, U.S. Customs Service
subfiles.to: Thomas J. Gorman, Deputy Commissioner of Customs
subfiles.about: The report traces a second cobalt shipment and records Metal & Ore Corporation's explanation for selling both lots to Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: Customs: another 227 bags of arsenical cobalt ore cleared November 16 for Mitsui; Haesler admitted selling to Mitsui before shipment, saying U.S. firms couldn't refine it and Canada blacklisted him.

subfiles.title: Duplicate clean copy of follow-up cobalt investigation
subfiles.from: Gordon H. Pike and E. J. Dougherty, U.S. Customs Service
subfiles.to: Thomas J. Gorman, Deputy Commissioner of Customs
subfiles.about: This duplicate records the investigation of the second Canadian cobalt shipment and the prior sale of the ore to Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: Clean copy: 227 bags weighing 124,030 pounds went to Mitsui; Metal & Ore couldn't find a U.S. refiner, the Mitsui sale predated shipment, and Haesler was blacklisted by Canada.

subfiles.title: Duplicate clean copy of the initial cobalt-shipment report
subfiles.from: Gordon H. Pike, U.S. Customs Service
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Investigations and Patrol
subfiles.about: This duplicate traces the first 378 bags of Canadian cobalt concentrate from importation to export aboard the Asosan Maru.
subfiles.summary: Clean copy of the initial report: five Canadian lots, 378 bags passed to Mitsui and the Asosan Maru, with a later 227-bag entry still to be investigated.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum forwarding the Treasury cobalt investigation
subfiles.about: The memorandum circulates the Treasury Department's reports on cobalt shipped from Canada through the United States to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum forwarding Gaston's December 31 letter and New York Customs reports on an apparent cobalt transshipment to Japan.

subfiles.title: William R. Thom's request for information on the embargo of war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: William R. Thom, U.S. House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Representative Thom asks what the government has done to embargo shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: William Thom asks for a report on restrictions on war-material exports to Japan so he can answer constituents.

subfiles.title: First draft reply to Representative Thom on export restrictions
subfiles.about: The draft explains the licensing system governing strategic exports and the commodities barred from shipment outside favored regions.
subfiles.summary: Draft reply to Thom: licenses favor the British Empire and Western Hemisphere; aviation fuel and scrap iron are not exported elsewhere, and aircraft materials are denied to countries bombing civilians.

subfiles.title: Second copy of draft reply to Representative Thom
subfiles.about: This duplicate draft outlines U.S. licensing restrictions on the export of strategic materials to Japan and other destinations.
subfiles.summary: Second draft: controlled exports need licenses, priority goes to the British Empire and Western Hemisphere, and aircraft-related exports are denied to countries bombing civilians.

subfiles.title: Third copy of draft reply to Representative Thom
subfiles.about: This further copy gives the Department's standard explanation of strategic-export licensing restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Third draft: export licensing protects defense while favoring the British Empire and Western Hemisphere, with aviation fuel, scrap iron and aircraft materials barred elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Final reply to Representative Thom concerning exports to Japan
subfiles.to: William R. Thom, U.S. House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Hull sends official information and supporting materials on U.S. restrictions governing war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Final reply to Thom: licensing favors the British Empire and Western Hemisphere, aviation fuel and scrap iron can't go elsewhere, and aircraft exports are barred to countries bombing civilians.

subfiles.title: Telegram on proposed Costa Rican exchange of scrap rails for locomotives
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, American Legation, San José
subfiles.about: Costa Rica's president asks the Department's view of a proposed exchange that would ultimately send discarded railway rails to Mitsui in Japan.
subfiles.summary: A Japan-connected agent offers Costa Rica two locomotives for 2,950 tons of scrap rails, probably bound for Mitsui; the president withholds approval pending an American answer.

subfiles.title: Reply on the Costa Rican scrap-rail transaction
subfiles.about: The Department explains the licensing implications and political risks of sending Costa Rican scrap rails through the United States to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reply: scrap export licenses are normally confined to Britain and the Western Hemisphere, in-transit cargo could still reach Japan unlicensed, and the legation should warn Costa Rica's president of public reaction.

subfiles.title: Instruction to London concerning alleged British armament production for Japan
subfiles.about: The Department requests information about a report that a British munitions factory was producing armaments for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Instruction asks London to investigate an allegation that a British factory makes armaments for Japan, amid a reported workers' strike threat.

subfiles.title: M.P. Fears British Factory Makes Arms for Japan
subfiles.from: Washington Post, copyrighted to The New York Times
subfiles.about: The clipping reports a British parliamentarian's concern that a munitions factory might be producing armaments for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Edwards sought an explanation from Churchill about alleged munitions manufacture for Japan, which workers opposed.

subfiles.title: Evidence of abnormal Japanese purchases of warlike supplies in the United States
subfiles.about: The table compares earlier annual Japanese purchases with much larger purchases during the first nine months of 1940.
subfiles.summary: Table of abnormal Japanese purchases in the U.S., including carbon black at ten times normal, rubber, zinc, steel and copper wire, as evidence of strategic stockpiling.
